subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS OVER 45 IN FEDERAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing, during the current session of parliament, legislation that would facilitate the employment, in federal works, undertakings, or businesses, as defined in section 2 of chapter 38 of the Statutes of Canada, 1956, or in any corporation, set up to perform some function or duty on behalf of the government of Canada, of male or female persons over 45 years of age who, on account of their age, find it difficult to secure employment at the present time.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that this year, at last, this notice of motion, which has been on the order paper every year since 1956, has reached the stage where it can be discussed. Like every member of this house, since my election to this parliament, I have realized in my encounters with the voters of my constituency, the workers of my riding, heads of families who tell us of their problems, that unfortunately there is in this country a discrimination against workers of 45 years of age and over.
In my opinion, that discrimination against workers 45 years of age and over is as reprehensible as racial and other discriminations.
Since I had the opportunity to become aware of the problem facing workers 45 years of age and over, I decided to consider the question with a view to know if the government could not do something to stop that discrimination in our country. That situation is caused by factors fairly numerous, but I shall mention only two.
Our industrialists-perhaps for want of leadership from the government, perhaps because of automation or other related problems-prefer to hire young people rather than persons of a certain age, feeling that young employees will adapt themselves more easily than older ones.
Another factor also causes this discrimination. It is the question of portable old age pensions. That question was discussed many times in this house, and I have no intention of bringing it back tonight. I merely wished to recall it to the attention of the house.
I was saying a while ago that, faced with this problem, I had wanted to go more deeply into it. I therefore studied what was done to stop this discrimination in other countries and especially in the American states.

Labour Conditions
Therefore, I welcome this opportunity for all of us to discuss this motion I have put before this house since 1956. The fact that we have not had an opportunity to discuss the matter since 1958 does not mean that I did not raise the question in this house. Every year in the debate on the labour department estimates, I appealed to the Minister of Labour and to the government to introduce a legislation providing for the removal of that discrimination.
The problem facing the worker who is 45 years of age or over is well known to all members of this house. It is a very serious problem and ever since I put it before the house, I received each year many representations from people all across Canada who are bent on making a stand against that discrimination.
Today, I would like to read into the official record of the house excerpts from some letters I have received.
In April 1960, I received from Mr. Xavier Lefebvre, to whom the civil service commission in Montreal had refused employment on account of his age, a letter in which he said:
I hope my government will help people over 45 to get employment In the service of our country.
A Mrs. Routhier, also of Montreal, complained also that she had been unable to secure employment on account of her age. Here is what she wrote me on July 10, 1959:
I worked as a bilingual private secretary for over 10 years. At the present time, there is an age limit, due in part to pension funds, which means that if you were not lucky enough to start working for some companies before reaching a certain age which entitles you to a pension upon retirement, you are refused employment because you are too old.
Last week I received a letter from Mr. Armand Couture of Montreal, in which he said:
-an individual 60 years old or more is too old to work-
Mr. Couture complained also about the fact that government authorities could have such a queer philosophy, and he added ironically:
At 60, a man is too old to do something good and useful for his country.
Mr. Speaker, other public men have reacted against such discrimination and to support this, I should like to quote none other than the former premier of Ontario, Mr. Frost, who stated, according to the newspaper Le Droit in its issue of March 10, 1959:

We should seriously consider this situation where some people cannot get employment, even in some provincial departments, because they are 40 years old or over. A man of 60 or even 65 may be as qualified as another who is under 40.
In 1959, the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) examined the question in the house and tried to find means of eliminating such discrimination.
The same year, Mr. Thomas Thomas, a
C.C.F. member of the Ontario legislature criticized the fact that one had to be less than 45 years old to pass an examination of the Ontario government or to get a job with the Department of Transport.
The C.C.F. leader in Ontario, Donald MacDonald, then suggested that legislation should be adopted at the provincial level to put an end to such discrimination against people 45 years of age or over.
The Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefen-baker) himself expressed concern about the situation in a speech he made not so long ago. I would be remiss if I did not quote the comments made by the Toronto daily Star on March 17, 1961, concerning that speech. The article reads as follows:
(Text):
The Prime Minister himself, an energetic 67, is a demonstration that a man over 60 is not necessarily ready for the shelf. While there are many who would like to see Mr. Diefenbaker sent into retirement by the electors, it is not because age has dimmed his faculties.
(Translation):
I do not have before me the latest statistics concerning the unemployed persons of 45 and over, but I have the official statistics for 1959 which were given to me by the Department of Labour. According to those statistics, there were, on January 17, 1959, 143,000 unemployed 45 years of age and over.
The present Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has given the problem his personal consideration, and according to the Ottawa Journal for May 8, 1959, he said:
(Text):
Labour minister Starr hopes to convince Canadian employers they are taking a shortsighted view on the question of older workers. ''I hope to be able to bring this home to employers across the country", he said in a Commons discussion Thursday of labour department spending estimates. He did not say how this would be done, beyond mentioning that the department's economic research branch has been making studies of the problem. Some firms were placing "ridiculous" upper age limits on the persons they would employ. A few companies would not hire anyone older than 35, Mr. Starr said it was a "downright fallacy" to think that younger workers were always to be preferred. It was also poor economics.

(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, by these few examples, I think I helped the house realize that a means must be found to check such discrimination. It is not enough, as the Minister of Labour has done, to make recommendations to the employers of this country. The government of Canada must take the lead in passing legislation that will eliminate such discrimination in the sector of our economy under the federal administration.
I confess that for the last few years a serious effort has been made in order to convince Canadian employers and Canadian industrialists to do something in order to cope with this problem. With this end in view, I wish to quote a few pamphlets one of which was published by the unemployment insurance commission in 1959. This publication was addressed to Canadian employers and said:
Our national employment service branches throughout Canada report that employers tend to increasingly recognize the advantage of hiring older workers.
The reason for that is quite simple.
Thanks to their skill and experience the output of mature workers is of better quality and brings in higher profits for the employer.
Therefore, if we are asking to consider the advisability of hiring older men and women who are able to work efficiently, it is not so much for humanitarian reasons (those people are not asking for charity), but we are rather trying to appeal to your sound business acumen.
The civil service commission authorities themselves, in a report submitted to the House of Commons in July 1960, agreed not to impose any age limit except for serious reasons.
Through a series of spot announcements employers in all the Canadian provinces were invited by the national employment office to hire middle-aged workers. It was said, among other things:
It is too bad that so many Canadian men and women are denied the right to earn their living because of their age, for the simple reason that the employer prefers younger persons.
Another spot announcement released in 1959 went as follows:
If you hire an employee over 40 years, you will be sure of getting an experienced, mature and responsible person.
These examples show that efforts were exerted by the unemployment insurance commission and by the Department of Labour as well, in order to urge Canadian employers not to discriminate against workers aged 45 or more.
Labour Conditions
On the other hand, I submit that that is not sufficient. Decisive steps must be taken in order to stop such discrimination and I feel that the government would do well to enact as soon as possible a piece of legislation which would solve this problem.
Such legislative steps have been taken by some American states, comprising New York. Indeed, in June 1958, that state enacted a law similar to the ones which were already in force in Pennsylvania, Rhode Island and Massachusetts.
Here is what the newspaper Dimanche Matin of June 15, 1958, had to say in connection with this law:
Under the provisions of the new New York law, it is illegal for a prospective employer to require an applicant to state his age. Moreover, the usual tag: "Age 21 to 35" will no more be allowed in classified ads appearing in daily or weekly newspapers, on the radio or on T.V. It will also be forbidden to advertise for a person under 45 years of age, as we often see in the newspapers.
Employers will not be allowed, in future, to mention any age in their ads in newspapers, magazines, periodicals, etc. The words: "Young man" and "Young girl" will also be forbidden.
Private employers as well as public and other employers will be required, in future, to accept applications from unemployed persons under or over 45 years of age and consider them on their merit.
The government would be well advised to seek inspiration from laws passed by various American states and by eastern Germany in 1959, with a view to preventing discrimination.
As I said earlier, what the government and members of this house can do in order to solve this problem would be, first of all, to set an example to Canadian employers and provincial governments by passing a legislation that would condemn any policy of discrimination in fields coming under the government's jurisdiction.
This legislation could apply to different sectors of the economy which come under the government's purview and are defined as follows in section 2, chapter 38, of the Statutes of Canada, 1956:
(i)	works, undertakings or business operated or carried on for or in connection with navigation and shipping, whether inland or maritime, including the operation of ships and transportation by ship anywhere in Canada;
(ii)	railways, canals, telegraphs and other works
(iii)	lines of steam and other ships connecting a province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of a province;
(iv)	ferries between any province and any other province or between any province and any country other than Canada;
(v)	aerodromes, aircraft and lines of air transportation;
(vi)	radio broadcasting stations;
(vii)	banks and banking;

Labour Conditions
And the different crown corporations such as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Trans-Canada Air Lines, as well as all the corporations established by the Canadian parliament.
I feel that, in so doing, the federal government would set an example not only for private enterprise but also for our various provincial legislatures.
After such a measure had been passed, it would be a good thing to call a federal-provincial conference to discuss whether it would be advisable for the provinces to follow in the footsteps of the Canadian parliament so that in each of them there would be legislation prohibiting all forms of discrimination towards persons and workers of 45 years and over.
That legislation should provide severe penalties for employers who do not obey it. I am also thinking of the suggestion submitted a few years ago by the hon. member for Oxford that a tax deduction be granted to industries employing a certain number of workers aged 45 and over. I think that that suggestion should be taken into consideration.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to appeal to every hon. member in this house, regardless of their party to become conscious of that problem and, by supporting this notice of motion, to ask the government, and especially the Minister of Labour, to introduce at this session legislation conceived to remove that discrimination.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS OVER 45 IN FEDERAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take up too much of the time of this house, but I want to take advantage of the debate on this notice of motion presented by the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) to support the remarks he has just made in this house.
Being myself a working man, I have been in a position to notice on the spot, as he did, the problem that arises in our economy today because citizens 45 years old and over cannot easily find employment in our country.
This is an unfortunate situation because in plants employees 45 years of age and over are usually the most qualified to do the work, and I feel that their experience and steadiness deserve to be taken into consideration.
I am of the opinion that it would be fully to the advantage of our industry to give special attention to the workers 45 years old and over.
I think that those people, more so than anybody else, have their employer's interests at heart. Through their experience and the work they have done in the past, I think they render the employer and the businessman a service that cannot be expected from a young
[Mr. Rouleau.)
man starting in this kind of work. The young man's assets are his spirit, his energy, his good will, but on the other hand he has against him his lack of experience in many fields and sometimes he is not serious enough.
I, myself, had the experience of directing groups of men at work, and I can assure the house that it is much easier to direct men of 45 years and over and obtain from them a reasonable maximum effort.
Mr. Speaker, this notice of motion from the hon. member for Dollard deserves to be considered by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). I invite him to think it over and I beg the members and the government to consider in more detail the case of our citizens who find it difficult now to get employment because of their age.
That also underlines the fact that very often, our citizens who are compelled to retire at the age of 65, cannot maintain a reasonable standard of living because of the small pension they receive. That is why pressure is brought to bear more and more on our legislators so that the age at which a person can receive the old age pension be lowered to 65. Thus, those Canadians could, at the time they retire, have a sufficient income and enjoy the same standard of living as their fellow citizens.
The members of our group support the motion introduced by the hon. member for Dollard and, in my opinion, the government should take it into consideration.
If our economy were healthier, I am sure we would easily find some employment for those people and would gladly give them some work.
As a proof of that, one merely has to recall the war years. At that time, even people over 70 had permanent employment to help meet our needs. I feel that if we were in a similar situation today, we would once again call upon those people to fill the vacancies on the labour market.
Without further ado, I wish to assure the hon. member for Dollard of the wholehearted support of our group.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS OVER 45 IN FEDERAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity today to say a few words on this most serious problem which is highlighted by the motion presented by the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau). This is a very serious problem.

It is not only serious but it is a growing problem, and not only a growing problem but an inevitable one. As sure as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west each and every one of us, if we live long enough, will reach the age of 45 and then we will become eligible for the dubious treatment that people 45 and over are accorded in this country at the present time, and have been in the past.
Men and women who are able to offer another 20 or 25 years of excellent service to their country find themselves in the position where, if they become unemployed, in far too many cases they are unable to get employment. Why is this so? The reason simply is that they have reached the age of 45 or over.
I think we should look first of all at why these people find themselves out of work. I would say that in this changing world certainly the main cause is automation, because we must remember that if they are 45 years old they must have been providing for their livelihood for some 20, 25 or possibly 30 years. Why then should they find themselves unemployed at the age of 45 or over? In my view automation is certainly one of the reasons. Automation, of course, and its effect on these people 45 years of age or over is one problem we have never come to grips with in this country.
But it is not enough to know the reason why so many people of this age are unemployed. I think we should also examine the reasons why they remain unemployed. As I have said, most people of 45 years of age are still able to give many years of service to their country and are well able to carry on whatever duties may be assigned to them. I have talked to many employers across the country who are more than willing to employ people of this age because they have attributes that they did not have when they were 20 or 25 years younger. Why is it not possible for employers who are willing to employ these people to do so? I think we will find that one of the major reasons is that throughout the country today there is a great hodgepodge of pension plans which are mostly under the jurisdiction of private insurance companies and it is not profitable for an insurance company to insure a person of that age. These people do not have enough years left for private insurance companies to set up a plan that will be profitable.
Therefore what we really have is a situation where people have 20 or 25 years left during which they could provide for their own livelihood and that of their children, if they still have to do so, and could be employed with profit to the employer, but they cannot get work because of the hodgepodge of pension plans we now have. As I say, this is one of the major reasons for the present discrimination.
Labour Conditions
If we cast our eyes ahead to resolution no. 33 on the order paper we will see there one that I hope to have the opportunity to introduce during this session. This resolution provides for a portable pension plan under which the benefits could be carried from job to job. I believe this would solve the problem we are discussing much better than the resolution before us today. However, that is another debate and I hope we will have the opportunity to debate that issue in the house.
It does no good just to wring our hands, feel sorry for these people and say something should be done. It is obvious that industry is unable to cope with the problem. Up to now at least it has certainly been obvious that no government this country has had has been able to cope with the problem, but I do say that there is a need for government to take the lead in this field. I believe that once government takes the lead it will not be too long before industry will start to follow; but industry will not do anything as long as it has the excuse that the government has not done anything about the matter.
One of the disadvantages that I see in the motion now before the house is that even if it were passed by the house and put into effect it would apply to a greater degree in certain areas of the country than in others. Certainly government projects are not evenly distributed throughout the country. However, Mr. Speaker, I wish to provide an opportunity for other hon. members to speak on this very important matter. Therefore I will conclude by saying that I should like to compliment the hon. member for Dollard on introducing this resolution which is good as far as it goes, and having regard to that fact we heartily support it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree that the problem of the older worker is one that requires the very careful attention and serious consideration of the government. The subject has been discussed in this house many times. The first time I recall it being discussed was on a motion moved by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). Since that time the subject has been discussed on several occasions. I believe that the question of legislation is secondary to that of the education of the public to the ability of the older worker to do a job which is equal to, and in many cases, better than the younger worker. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has taken a number of steps to improve the public knowledge of what the older worker can do. Some of these studies have been referred to by the hon. member who introduced the motion as well as by other hon. members. I think the Minister of Labour himself is

Labour Conditions
convinced from the actions he has taken and the studies that have been undertaken, that the older worker does have a difficult problem. He has made this statement in the house on many occasions.
There are two main points upon which I would agree with the mover of this motion. First, there is in this country an age discrimination against the older worker. Second, pension problems are, to some extent, responsible for the fact that the older worker does have difficulty in securing a job. There is a great deal of misunderstanding, but I think a lot of that misunderstanding has been cleared up by several of the studies to which I will refer that were instituted by the minister.
The first, and I think most effective study that was made is reported upon in a document entitled, "The Aged Worker in the Canadian Economy". This report was published by the economics and research branch of the Department of Labour. The booklet contains a very thorough study of the incidence of labour problems amongst the aged. The report does not purport to come to a conclusion on the problem except to indicate that the problem of the older worker is going to increase as time goes on because of the increase in the life expectancy of the individual.
However, some other studies have certainly shown the fallacy of the belief that the older worker is incompetent. I should like to refer to a small pamphlet entitled, "2 Minutes of Employment Facts." This is a series published by the Department of Labour, and this issue concerns age and performance in the retail trade. I should like to quote briefly from this pamphlet:
A large part of the continuing campaign to reduce the employment problems of older workers must necessarily be devoted to refuting the mistaken ideas and the prejudice which so often create artificial barriers against the hiring of workers over 40. Such ideas can be countered only by presenting to employers the proven facts about the abilities and qualities of older workers. To add to the store of such basic information, the economics and research branch of the Department of Labour, on the request of the interdepartmental committee on older workers, undertook a survey in the retail trade-an industry which employs more than ten per cent of Canadian workers and stands third among all the industries in the employment it provides.
I do not intend to read the whole pamphlet, but there is one paragraph which indicates the general trend of the report.
The study showed, first of all, that the older sales employee has at least as good a record of performance as the younger employee, with those over 46 having a better than average performance record. Peak performance seems to be reached between the ages of 51 and 55.

Then, there is a similar pamphlet entitled, "Pension Plans and the Employment of Older Workers.,, On this particular point, I agree with the hon. member for Timmins when he says that the portability of pensions is one of the matters that can bring about some relief for the older worker. I believe that many employers hesitate to take on people who will actuarially increase the cost of the pension scheme that they have set up. This particular pamphlet reads in part as follows:
Most obstacles to the employment of older workers and to their retention in employment must sooner or later diminish for they are based on nothing more substantial than prejudice.
Then, there is a report entitled, "The Efficiency of the Aged." This study also was instigated by the Minister of Labour. He sent out a number of letters to employers around the country, and a significant part of the report reads as follows:
In almost every case, the replies to these letters indicated that the hiring practices in firms engaged in clothing manufacture were based not only on age but simply on whether the job applicant could perform the work involved. As one company spokesman stated, our company has never taken into consideration the age of the person to be employed as we are more interested in the qualifications and abilities of our employees.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, that all employers in this country, including the federal and provincial governments, would adopt this as a basis for employment, that is the ability of the person to do the job, and not his age. If that principle were generally accepted, then the problem we have before us today would not be nearly as great. There are many occupations, and I think they are obvious, in which the older worker is actually much better than the younger worker. A job which requires the stability and care of an older worker means that he will be more efficient in that job.
There are many other studies, Mr. Speaker, and undoubtedly there are other hon. members who would like to speak on this subject. I would merely say, in conclusion, that I agree with the principle that the older worker must be given some special consideration. Whether or not the adoption of this resolution would result in the achievement of this desirable result, I do not know. I do know that the Minister of Labour has undertaken many studies and published the information in many pamphlets sent out by the Department of Labour to bring to the attention of the public the fact that the older worker can be just as efficient as the younger worker. I feel if this point can be impressed upon the public, it will be more effective than legislation which is, in essence, compulsory.

speechtext: If I thought there was no one else who wished to speak [DOT]on this subject and we could have a vote, I would be happy to forgo my speech. I take it, however, that the hon. member for Bow River desires to speak.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS OVER 45 IN FEDERAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: Yes, I do.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS OVER 45 IN FEDERAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
In that event, we would be denied the opportunity of having a vote on this matter. Since that is the case, perhaps as the representative of one of the major industrial ridings in our country I would be expected to say a word on this important subject. The hon. member who has just spoken said the particular recommendations made in this resolution might not be the way to effect a settlement of this problem. In any event, I am sure we all agree that the proposer of the resolution has served a useful purpose in bringing this question to the attention of the Minister of Labour, of the government, and of the house. This is a serious subject. Admittedly, this has presented a serious problem in our country for many years. It is not one which has arisen only since the present government came into being, nor is that the suggestion made by the proposer of the resolution which is now before us. It is a symptom of our time; it is a symbol of a stage in the development of our society. Nevertheless, it presents a challenge. Our technological advance has increased the severity of the situation and made a solution more urgent than ever.
We all recall the existence in our country of what are called "Forty five and over" clubs in which men in that age group formed themselves into an association for the purpose of impressing governments at all levels with the desirability of taking their plight into account. It is easy for us, when we are dealing with broad issues, when we are dealing with statistics, to overlook the human tragedy involved in many of the stories behind the statistics, behind the generalizations, behind the broader pictures that we paint in our statements in this house. It is a fact that there are thousands of people in this country who because of their age are denied an opportunity to work. Age is not the only reason in many instances, but in many instances it is the reason. We see evidence of this in the number of people who move from one job to another.
I have in my own riding now an engineer from one of the best universities in this country, who only ten days ago was given notice that his services with a particular company would no longer be required-not because his services were not valuable, but because there would no longer be need for his particular skills, automation having replaced them. Now
Labour Conditions
he is out on the street and he has been told by two prospective employers that they cannot give him work, simply because he is over a certain age. Now, this is a tragedy. It is a tragedy for that man. It is a tragedy for his family and it is bound to have its consequences on our society.
Some progress has been made, notably by voluntary effort, toward mitigating the severity of this serious social and economic situation. Among the unemployed in our country we find many men and women in this particular age category who are unable to obtain employment. It has been suggested that if something were done about the portability of pensions the problem would be somewhat reduced. I believe we have got to do something about the portability of pensions though that, in itself, is not the real solution-it would merely be a provision, a necessary form of relief to men and women in this age group who cannot obtain work. Nevertheless, in the absence of a real solution it would afford some relief, and I think, therefore, it is desirable we should do something about it.
I do not think the government of the day has taken every step within its power to bring about the portability arrangement which would provide the kind of relief suggested. We have been talking about the portability of pensions, now, for three years in this house and no substantial progress has been made. If the government of the day wished, in co-operation with the provinces, to take the necessary steps to bring this about, it could be done. Undoubtedly there is a constitutional difficulty. It is not open to the federal government to make pensions portable from one province to another under the present provisions of section 91 of the British North America Act. That can only be brought about, of course, by the provinces agreeing to the necessary constitutional amendment, or through some co-operative arrangement being made between the two senior levels of government. I suggest, in a constructive way, to the Minister of Labour and to the Minister of Finance who has some residual interest in this matter, that this should be undertaken at the earliest possible moment.
The problem presented by the denial of work to people because of their age may have been aggravated by the increase in the life expectancy. We cannot avoid giving serious consideration to ways and means by which a solution can be effected. I am suggesting that the government now has at its disposal one of the vehicles by which we could make some indentation on the full consequences of this unfortunate situation. I draw attention to the joint and unanimous recommendations which were made by the special mission to

Labour Conditions
Europe of a group composed of Canadians from the productivity council representing various segments in our national life. After a study of conditions in Europe, that mission made a unanimous recommendation as to the course which should be followed in this country with respect to labour-management-government co-operation. That report must not be allowed to gather dust. In my judgment it is one of the most significant documents ever presented in this area to a government in this country.
The productivity council recognized that production in Canada depends upon a number of factors. It recognized that among these factors was the distrust which persists in this country to an alarming degree between at least two of the partners in industry. In an effort directed to removing this mistrust, the council established this special mission to Europe. The mission visited a number of countries and examined the whole question of labour-management-government co-operation. I recommend to all hon. members of this house who have not yet had an opportunity of perusing this report to do so. It is made up of recommendations which represent the unanimous thinking of representatives of the Canadian Congress of Labour, men like Mr. Dodge, one of the vice presidents of that body; the president of the Goodrich Rubber Company, the president of the University of Western Ontario and others of this calibre. They reported that there was a serious gap between the extent of labour-management-government co-operation in this country as compared with the level of collaboration which prevails in this area in Europe. It will be noted that in Europe, particularly in countries like France and Sweden, special consideration is given to employees in certain age groups. Among these age groups is to be found consideration for the particular age group, or something like the particular age group referred to in this resolution. The employers and employees, backed up with leadership and support given by government, take into account the economic and social dislocation that results from putting people out of work because of age as well as other factors.
We do not do anything like this in this country. I am not blaming the government. I am not dealing with the problem in a narrow, political way, because it is too important, in my judgment, to receive this particular interpretation. I am seeking to address myself to the problem in the light of the fact that it exists, has existed, and something must be done about it. I feel that in the recommendations made by the special commission to Europe of the productivity

council something can be done, if labour, management and government sitting together, not in positions of distrust and antagonism, but each recognizing that each has a responsibility and a right to participate in industry, along with the community. Something can be done if we will address ourselves to all the problems involved; this is one of the problems.
I should like to see the Minister of Labour take the lead in this situation. I know he is interested in it; I know he has been interested in it for a number of years. I know he would have done something about it a few years ago if it had not been for the intransigent position taken by certain of his colleagues in the government who were opposed to setting up the kind of instrument for co-operation about which I have been speaking.
I make that statement knowing it to be the case. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka nods his head. I hope he is not making a political nod. But I am saying this problem was before the government two years ago. I hope, nothing having been done then, that with the inspiration which has been given by this unanimous report of the special commission to Europe named by the productivity council the particular machinery suggested will be used to address itself to this problem and to many other problems which we have in our country and which have such a definite relation to an improvement in the relations between the various partners in industry, an improvement which has a very definite bearing, in my judgment, on the improvement of economic conditions in our country.
I think that the hon. member who has proposed this resolution has done a worth while service in bringing to the attention of the house the existence of this problem.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this resolution I would first like to join with all other hon. members who have spoken this afternoon in congratulating the hon. member for Dollard for presenting the resolution. It is always difficult to follow the hon. member for Essex East in that regard, having to decide what side of the fence he was really on. But I would like to ask him, could the federal government at the present time bring in legislation to cover what the resolution asks for; and if so, how are we going to enforce that act in question? I come back to the original premise with which I started. Who was it brought in the productivity council? Who was it brought in vocational training? Those are the people-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, at five o'clock I had just said that the government had established a fantastic record of deceit and it had shown complete lack of integrity.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: And I said it was false.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member who interrupted me said it was false, and I intend to put the evidence on the record. The evidence I intend to put on the record is a statement which was given just a short while ago by the Leader of the Opposition on the subject of foreign exchange reserve losses, with which we are concerned. He said:
The information made available by the government late on Friday, in response to a Liberal motion, for the day-to-day losses of foreign exchange demonstrates conclusively that the exchange emergency began before the election and was hidden by the government. It shows that a rapid loss of exchange began on April 30, which was apparently temporarily halted by the pegging of the Canadian dollar at $0,921 on May 3; that a second rapid loss of exchange began on May 31 and continued to June 4; and a third rapid loss began on June 12 and continued throughout the week before the general election on June 18. The greatest loss for any single day before the election was the loss on June 12, two days before the Prime Minister's final election telecast. The statement by the ex-minister of finance to the Canadian club in Toronto on October 1 that "it was not until the third full week of June that the average daily loss of reserves rose to serious proportions" is therefore not true. Serious losses began at the beginning of June and intensified on June 12. On October 2 the Prime Minister stated: "The intensification in the loss of exchange started in earnest on the fifteenth. The sixteenth was a Saturday, the seventeenth a Sunday. These figures tell their story and answer

Ways and Means
once and for all the allegation that we had anything to conceal during the month of June that we did not place before the Canadian people."
When the Leader of the Opposition asked the Prime Minister why he did not mention any aspect of the foreign exchange crisis in his broadcast to the Canadian people of June 14, the Prime Minister replied:
Because as I have pointed out, the situation was not serious then.
Now listen to this.
The figures supplied by the government, which we now have before us, show a total loss

That is to say, deliveries of exchange to the market.
-of $50 million on May 31, June 1 and June 4, three successive business days; and a loss of $35.3 million on June 12; a loss of $17.4 million on June 13; $17 million on June 14. Or, a total of almost $70 million in the three days before the Prime Minister's last campaign telecast. In fact, the loss on June 15, when the Prime Minister said the loss "started in earnest", was not as great as it was on June 12. In other words, the government tried to conceal the facts of the crisis from the people before the election, and from parliament afterwards.
Just nonsense.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Those facts are contained in the return, and they have been disclosed on the initiative taken by the opposition. The government has been obliged to furnish the evidence. The figures released on Friday do not tell the whole story because they do not reveal the government's foward trading on the foreign exchange market; but they do leave no doubt that the country was facing acute exchange losses throughout April and early May, and again from the end of May onward to June 18. So I conclude that I have every right to say what I did before five o'clock-that the government has deceived the house and the Canadian people.
I return now to the statement made by the Minister of Finance when beginning the debate. That clearly shows that even at this late hour there is no sign of improvement on the part of the government's attitude. The new minister used the same approaches, the same distortions to hide the real facts of the economic affairs of our country, and he showed the same lack of understanding of our difficulties which was so typical of his arrogant predecessor. The only difference between the two is that the minister was more candid and more succinct in his statement than his long-winded predecessor, the new Minister of Justice. The new Minister of Finance, however, had the audacity to say that 1962 will be the most prosperous year in our history.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Wait till you hear this. On the basis of such an erroneous statement, how

can he expect to be taken seriously, not only by this house but by the country? What are the facts? For the first three quarters of 1962; unemployment has remained, on the average, at 6.2 per cent, which is exactly what it has been since 1957, as compared to 3 per cent between 1947 and 1957. Moreover, in spite of the temporary recovery in 1962-and here is another barometer-our gross national product in constant dollars per capita will be lower than it was in 1956. Since this is the best measure of our progress and prosperity, how can the minister justify his own statement?
What is the true picture and the true barometer of the economic situation of the country at the moment? Mr. Chairman, it can be summarized under three heads. First, 1962, like 1959, will be the peak of the short cycle. Second, 1963 like 1960, will mark the beginning of another recession-
Doom.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -of another pause or of another slowdown.
And gloom.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Third, when those cyclical forces are put to one side we realize that the Canadian economy continues to suffer from stagnation as well as from structural unemployment. I challenge the Minister of Finance to find any impartial observer of the economic scene who will disagree with that general statement I have just made. And yet the minister, in his statement, chose to boast about the immediate past instead of announcing new policies designed to meet the difficulties of the immediate future. This government will never learn how to do its job efficiently and properly.
I remember very well what happened in 1960, particularly in the month of April, when the Leader of the Opposition warned the former minister of finance that we were on the eve of another recession and asked him what he intended to do about it, just as we are asking now about 1963 and being interrupted by those jeers. Listen to what the then minister of finance had to say, as reported on page 3167 of Hansard for April 12, 1960:
The Leader of the Opposition was so anxious this afternoon to get everybody talking recession with him he was in effect asking the Minister of Finance what preparations he was making for the next recession. The best preparation that can be made for the next recession is to continue the present government in office.
Well, this was, as I stated, on April 12, 1960, and we all know now that when the minister was making this silly, arrogant statement the recession was starting, that it continued until the end of the first quarter of

1961, and that the government did absolutely nothing to prevent or to minimize it. I doubt whether many of the ministers who sit on the other side of the chamber even knew that it existed. Today we are in the same position. Today we are in exactly the same position as that in which we were then. All impartial observers agree that there will be a slowdown in 1963. In August-and that is not so long ago-the President of the United States told the United States people that such was the outlook and that the United States government was already making preparations to minimize that recession. What do we get from the government in Canada? They boast about the past but they refuse to plan for the immediate future. They even refuse to look at it. That is another reason why we on this side of the chamber have no confidence whatsoever in this government. We have no confidence in this government, not only because of its lack of integrity, as I showed a moment ago, but also because of its failure to understand and to deal with our economic difficulties. After what I have put on the record I ask you, Mr. Chairman, this question: How can anyone explain the conduct of my friends over to my left? I refer to the Social Credit party who, notwithstanding their charges, systematically voted to uphold this government. I ask the committee to listen to this and to note the attitude of the Minister of Finance on this matter when, as reported at page 336 of Hansard, he stated as follows:
The Social Credit party, according to its pronouncements, stands fairly and squarely on its principle of supporting the maintenance of private enterprise in this country. This government does likewise, Mr. Speaker. In the division which this house saw the other evening you saw a division on principle. You saw parties supporting private enterprise on the one hand, and the socialists and pseudo-socialists divided against them on the other.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance has not even made reference to the stagnant state of our economy and to the abnormal unemployment situation inflicted upon us since 1957.
The banks are to be blamed for it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We have stated a number of times-and I wish to repeat it once again- that the volume of our national production, per capita, has increased by 22 per cent from 1949 to 1956, but that it has gone down by 4 per cent since 1956.
Mr. Chairman, that is the most undeniable indication of the present stagnation of our economy, even if the government does not want to face this evidence.

Ways and Means
What is the cause of that stagnation?
The chartered banks.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the detailed consideration of our public accounts has brought it out to us very clearly.
Our national production or our national expenditures have gone up by 8 per cent only from 1957 to 1961.
Now, of the four groups which make up the total expenditures of the nation-
Plus interest.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
*-consumers' expenditures have increased by 14 per cent while government expenditures and exports have respectively gone up by 15 per cent. Since these three classes of expenditures have gone up almost twice as fast as our total national production or expenditures, they cannot be the direct cause of the inadequate increase of our total production or expenditures during that period.
Then, there are the expenditures due to private investments. This fourth class of expenditures has gone down by 19 per cent since 1957. So that is the obvious reason of our stagnation. Expenditures, relating to housing construction and non residential construction, as well as purchases of industrial machinery and equipment have decreased by 19 per cent and that is why our total production or expenditures have gone up by only 8 per cent. That is the clear and simple explanation of our inadequate economic growth since 1957. We have said so to the government several times, but they would not listen to us.
The Liberal policy put forward in this house by the Leader of the Opposition, as well as by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon), clearly shows what we could do to put a stop to the present stagnation.
I only want to mention briefly some of the points of that program.
First, put a stop to monetary restrictions and lower the interest rates. This will immediately create conditions likely to increase investments.
Where are you going to get the money?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Second, establish a loan fund for the municipalities so that they be truly able to invest in all building activities required for the improvement of local services.
With or without interest?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Third, increase and extend the financial share of the federal government in slum clearing and urban renewal projects, which will bring about a considerable increase of such forms of investment as the building of healthier housing units.

Fourth, demand from the industrial development bank that it concentrate its activities and services on underprivileged areas, so as to stimulate more extensive investments in those areas.
Where are you going to find the money?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
And lastly, grant specific tax exemptions to any business which wants to expand and, if necessary, as the Leader of the Opposition suggested before, establish a national economic development fund which would be entrusted with investment promotion arrived at by private enterprise.
There you have, Mr. Chairman, the attitude of the Liberals on the one hand, which is quite clear, with a program designed for everyone, which could be carried out at once, and on the other hand the stagnation program of the Conservatives.
Promises again.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But in all this, Mr. Chairman, there is one attitude which remains mysterious: it is that of the Social Crediters. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

How can the Social Crediters reconcile their vote in this house with their conscience? They know very well that this Conservative government has nothing new to offer. They acknowledge it themselves in their speeches. Why then-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, for the last half hour this chamber has listened to the representations made by the former member for Stormont, now the member for Laurier, the new Ontario leader in Quebec, concerning the economic situation which reigns in Canada at present. We have listened to the hon. member for Laurier tell us that this government of which I am a member deliberately deceived the people during the campaign that led up to the general election. I belonged to this government before June 18, Mr. Chairman, and I still belong to it.
In spite of what hon. members may say, we were elected as the government and I can say that we never deceived the people of Canada. The facts are there to indicate that this run on the Canadian dollar which prompted the measures taken on June 21 came about as a result of a phenomenon which took place between the dates of June 15 and June 21-

the month preceding that time a sum of only $128 million had been withdrawn. When hon. members say that we deceived the people they are lying to this chamber like they are lying to the people of Canada.
The measures that were taken were necessary and hon. members opposite know that very well. They were taken because any self-respecting government had to take such measures in order to protect the interests of the people whom they were pledged to serve. No, Mr. Chairman, there was no deceit in the action of the government. The only deceit that there is on record on the part of any Canadian government is the deceit that was perpetrated by the former administration, of which the hon. member for Stormont was a member, when in 1957 they deliberately concealed from the people a report which indicated that the economy indeed was sliding downwards, that a rise in unemployment was threatening and that a period of economic depression was probably looming.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I rise on a question of privilege. My question of privilege is this: I was not a member of this house from 1954 to 1957 and I am not the hon. member for Stormont, I am the hon. member for Laurier.

The hon. member can hardly deny that he was the hon. member for Stormont before he was the member for Laurier. But, Mr. Chairman, there was shameful deceit performed in 1957 by the Liberal government that preceded us. I listened to the hon. member for Laurier when he referred to the unemployment that still prevails in Canada. I listened to the tale of gloom and doom with which we have become so familiar in this chamber. I listened to the same story from the hon. member to which we listened for four long years from the opposite benches when we were told that everything in Canada was going to the dogs. Actually, they created unemployment because they scared so many people into shying away from the planned developments which would have added to prosperity.
We listened to this story from the hon. member for Laurier, but the facts are here to disprove him. It seems that for a country that is going into gloom and doom, things are not so bad now. I have before me the edition of Time for this week, and I shall read from it. I read this:
-Prime Minister John Diefenbaker, appearing an the C.B.C.'s Nation's Business last week, was emboldened to declare, characteristically, that "Canada now is enjoying one ol the greatest periods of economic progress in its peacetime history."
Then, the article continues:
Certainly, there was some reason to bask. The gross national product for the first time reached

an estimated $40 billion, a 7 per cent growth in the first nine months and well up to expectations. Ottawa economists saw permanent new muscle in manufacturing, which led all industry with a stable 2 per cent rise in 1962's second quarter, and continued strong into the third. Perhaps accounting more than anything else for the sense of well-being in board rooms was a 3 per cent rise in corporation profits to a record $3.9 billion- no less than 30 per cent above the wintry bottom of 1961. "We'll end the year firmly," predicted one Toronto bank economist. "The economy will level off a bit next year, but not much."
We hear talk about this austerity, this word which our friends opposite like to use so much. I continue to quote:
Despite the austerely high Bank of Canada rediscount rate (down to 5 per cent from June's 6 per cent), the bankers had particular cause to count blessings: bank loans rose in three months by $130 million to a record $6.7 billion by October 3.
Will you read the next paragraph?

Mr. Chairman, a few moments ago, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) spoke on unemployment and tried once more to scare the people of Canada, with the spectre of unemployment which was used by the Liberals as a scarecrow for four years.
The facts are there, Mr. Chairman, and I can prove it by reminding the house that in 1962, more Canadians are at work, earning better pay while putting more money aside than ever before in the history of Canada. The percentage of unemployment is 3.9 per cent and the number of unemployed has gone down to 280,000. Those, Mr. Chairman, are statistics which can hardly be denied by the hon. member for Laurier in spite of his cries of doom of a few moments ago.
Not only is the Canadian economy prosperous, but it has come out of the stagnation in which our hon. opposites had left it. Their negligence and maladministration had resulted in economic tension in this country. But fortunately, the Conservatives corrected the situation.
Our friends opposite mentioned the program which was outlined in the house by the Leader of the Opposition, in the course of the debate on the address. The commend-

able points of that program-as I have said and as I repeat-are copied in their entirety on what was done by the Conservative administration. The remaining good points in that program were borrowed from the New Democratic party by our Liberal friends, who, in their thirst for power are using all and any means they can.
But let us look at that program of which the member for Laurier has quoted a few points. What do we see? We note, for instance, that he has just found out that the Liberals intend to help Canadian municipalities; however, he seems to be forgetting that that is exactly what the Conservative government has been doing for four years. He seems to be forgetting that thanks to the winter works program, the Conservative government has provided employment for over 500,000 workers and paid out over $100 million to municipalities in the nation.
When they mention urban renewal and construction, the hon. members opposite seem to forget something. It is that through the steps taken by the Conservative government, the government of the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, over $2 billion were loaned to building contractors in the nation, allowing the construction of 800,000 new dwellings in Canada. They forget that thanks to the C.M.H.C. millions of dollars have been spent by the Conservative government for the urban renewal of which we were told a few moments ago by the hon. member for Laurier.
Where have they been these last four years? Were they so busy preaching gloom and doom, suffering and poverty that they remained unaware of what was taking place?
Mr. Chairman, listening to our friends opposite, especially the member for Laurier, we could think that if they ever get back into power they will establish a program of economic development which, according to them, will solve the problems that resulted from their own negligence under their own administration.
If we look at their program, we find that what is good has already been done whereas what has not been done is not good, that it is stamped with socialism, a socialism that has no place in a country like ours, that would impose a burden on our trade, in a country like ours which is in full economic development, which is experiencing an upsurge in free enterprise that will enable it to fulfil its destiny.
A while ago, the hon. member for Laurier criticized the Social Crediters because, according to him, they preach principles that resemble those of the Conservative party.
Ways and Means
Mr. Chairman, I prefer men who try to find some good in principles based on logic to men who try to be more socialistic than the socialists themselves. They are firm in their beliefs whereas our Liberal friends opposite merely try to borrow from the socialist theories of the N.D.P. in the hope that that will be a stepping stone to power.
Mr. Chairman, I do not fully approve of the theories put forward by our Social Credit friends, but just the same I have some respect for those men who have come here to suggest forms of government and administration which perhaps deserve to be considered, and which are certainly preferable to the formulas proposed by our Liberal friends, formulas which would lead the Canadian nation to the deepest abyss of socialism, with all its miseries and distress, because we know what miseries and distress are prevalent in those countries where socialism has been adopted.
Mr. Chairman, I have heard my excellent friend, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), say that the Conservative party has no program and does not go forward. The hon. member does not seem to have read the speech from the throne.
What does the hon. member for Laurier think of the vigorous commercial promotion program already put under way with so much success by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), who has already succeeded, over a period of 18 months, to increase our exports to all countries of the world? What does the hon. member think of the measure adopted by the house, which doubles the amount of insurance on export credit?
What does he think of those commercial missions which are now travelling around the world and which, enlightened by the representatives of the Department of Trade and Commerce, manage to place orders in those countries which, before, used to sell to us rather than buy from us?
Mr. Chairman, this government has undertaken a sales campaign, which will inevitably bring here in Canada the orders which our business enterprises need and which will permit them to employ surplus labour which, unfortunately, is still unemployed perhaps in some areas.
Mr. Chairman, one should not overlook the fact that in a country like ours, inhabited by only 18 million citizens, which can produce four times more than its needs, one must go outside the country to find the necessary orders to maintain a continuous flow of business for our manufacturers and industrialists.

Ways and Means
The hon. member for Laurier says that we are doing nothing in anticipation of the future. Well, let him consider the measures that we propose in order to give some taxation relief to business enterprises engaged in scientific research.
Let him study the measure that we want to introduce in the house and through which we shall give once more a tax abatement to those business firms which, having increased the amount of their sales and made specific efforts to increase Canadian productivity, deserve the kind attention of the authorities.
The hon. member says that we do nothing for the unemployed. Well, let him consider what we have done with a view to promoting the construction of technical and professional training schools in Canada. He will realize that thanks to the efforts of the federal government, more than 400 projects have been started, at a cost of more than $270 million.
Mr. Chairman, it is a well known fact that the unemployed are found among the large family of day-labourers, and it is also established that those who can learn a trade can find a job as well.
To teach a profession to as many Canadians as possible is one of the aims of this Conservative government. That is one of the objectives we are now achieving and which will be pursued in the months and years ahead.
In another field, Mr. Chairman, for four whole years, our hon. friends have stated that our tax system should be revised. Well, a royal commission has now been appointed to study that taxation system so as fairly and equitably to distribute the tax burden to be borne by Canadians.
We want to develop our natural resources, our oil resources. We want to help the natural gas industry. We want to enter foreign markets to get orders for those products the sale of which is essential to the welfare of the Canadian nation. We want a program based on logic and common sense, and that is why we will be setting up an economic development board, on which the nation's best brains will serve. Together with the Canadian government those experts will apply themselves, in a spirit of fairness, progress and justice, to studying the circumstances which will not only enable the rational development of our natural resources and primary products, but give us the opportunity of treating those prim-
[Mr. SevignyJ
ary and secondary products at home, so that Canadians can use our processed natural resources in the shape of manufactured goods.
That board will be made up of the best experts of the Canadian nation, recruited in financial, industrial, academic and agricultural circles, and wherever people can be found who will enlighten us, who are willing to co-operate with us and work with us hand in hand, in order to build this Canadian nation, as we have been doing successfully for the past four years.
Mr. Chairman, thanks to this economic development council, which is to be established, we shall be able to develop underdeveloped areas in the Canadian nation. We shall see to it that industries are attracted to those areas, which will bring them that same prosperity which abundantly prevails in practically all the other parts of Canada.
What we want to do through this policy of ours is to give full employment to all Canadians, and to see that they earn money and improve a living standard which is already very high in this country.
We shall bring prosperity to the homes and families and with this system we shall do our duty-to serve the best interests of all Canadian citizens.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, thanks to that system, we Conservatives hope to protect the interests of all Canadian citizens, in whatever field of political activity we are operating.
Since coming to power, in June 1957, we have achieved definite results. For instance, let us examine what has been accomplished in the field of social security, and we shall see that the aged, the blind, the invalid and the veteran are better off.
Let us look at what has happened in the field of agriculture. Thanks to the dynamic leadership given by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton), today we have markets for our products, and our farmers in the east or the west will know that, due to the federal government's initiative, their products can be sold, their farms will no longer be at a standstill and continued progress will brighten up their horizon.
Look at what we did for our workers. Not only have we improved their lot we also found jobs for them.
That is why I say and I repeat that today more people are at work than at any time in the history of the Canadian nation.

Ways and Means
Through trade, we have spread Canada's name in markets abroad. We developed those markets and provided orders for the industries of the Canadian nation.
Fortunately, the Canadian people trusted us enough to keep us in power on June 18 and give us an opportunity to continue our effort launched June 10, 1957 and we will not relax our efforts until we obtain the desired results.
Mr. Chairman, we had expected in this debate a constructive criticism from our friends opposite.
(Text):
We thought, from the many speeches made by hon. members opposite concerning the economic situation of Canada, that possibly we would glean certain suggestions which would permit us to carry on with the work that we undertook nearly five years ago. But, unfortunately, all we heard was a repetition of what we heard just a moment ago from my hon. friend the member for Laurier; a story of gloom, a story of doom, predictions that 1963 would be frightful, a story which is meant to scare the Canadian people into the belief that with the Liberals things would be better. But actually the reality is that with the Liberals we would have an ultrasocialistic government, not based on the sincerity that would prevail if the hon. members from the New Democratic party were there, but an ultra-socialism based uniquely on a desire for power at all costs, irrespective of the consequences.
Mr. Chairman, socialism is bad. The program based on socialism which is advocated by hon. members opposite would cost so much money that the annual deficit would regularly exceed $1 billion, if it so happened that misfortune befell the Canadian people and my hon. friends opposite got into power.
My hon. friends opposite have no consideration for economic facts or principles. They go to the people with impracticable projects- projects which, for those who do not have facts and figures, may have a certain appeal, but programs which cannot be realized because of their cost and the means at the disposal of government. My hon. friends the Liberals are the same Liberals as those who in a particular province are at present advocating a program which would be so costly,
if it were ever executed the way they wish to execute it, that it would ruin the province in which they wish it executed.
Mr. Chairman, what must be done in sound and sane government is to face the facts, and face especially the reality of the facts, such as the Progressive Conservative government of the Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker has done during the last five years. We have the programs; we have the plans. But we made the programs and the plans, keeping in mind always that this programming must be based on the reality of the facts. Such is not the purpose of my hon. friends opposite. They criticize; they belittle all that is being done. In their mad desire for power they are unfortunately creating a reputation for Canada abroad which is unjustified for this great country. Last year, at the peak of their prophesies of gloom and doom, articles appeared in the British and French press in which the writers of the articles advised the people of their countries not to emigrate to Canada because, according to reports that were received from the politicians of this nation, things were bad in Canada.
All my hon. friends have achieved with their prophesies of gloom and doom is to increase their number of seats in this house compared with the number they held prior to June 18. But they did not achieve the end they desired, which was to cross the aisle and sit on this side of the chamber. The people of Canada know now that this government did not deceive the Canadian people. They realize the power of the facts which they can read in government publications and magazines, facts which they can get from the dominion bureau of statistics. The Progressive Conservative government of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker has given to this nation a form of government which has led us to our present state of prosperity, the highest state of prosperity ever achieved (Translation):
Mr. Chairman, because Canadians are wise, they like to face reality and wish to be told the truth above all, they will see to it that our friends opposite are kept in the opposition and the Conservative government on the front benches, because it has given them a dynamic and progressive political administration during the last four years, thanks to the program that you have all read in the speech from the throne. This government will lead our nation towards new progress, new prosperity, new understanding within our country and with all the other nations.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, thanks to that program, Canada's prestige will increase not only within our borders but also outside them.
