Mr. Chairman, I was saying that both the speech from the throne and the estimates we are now considering remind us that every aspect of the Canadian economy is affected, directly or indirectly, by government policy. Ottawa sets the pace not only for federal enterprises but for many local and provincial projects as well. That is why every decision that is made in this house is so vital to the welfare of the entire country. Ottawa, in turn, is subjected to external pressures and influences that make a significant impact upon policy-making in this capital. We have been made aware of this many times during the past month. In truth, we live in a period of rapid change that affects the deliberations of men everywhere in the democratic world. Only in this context can we hope to appreciate our own problems and our own opportunities.
We may remind ourselves that we are the products of the revolutions of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, both political and industrial. This includes the French and American revolutions, and of course our own struggle for responsible government in Upper and Lower Canada just a little over one hundred years ago. The idea that the poor man and the stupid man have the same right to respect and to happiness as the rich man and the clever man is a powerful concept that is moving people everywhere as never before in world history. Why should we look with disapproval or distrust upon millions of men and women in Africa and Asia who take seriously the same battle cries of liberty, equality and fraternity that stirred Europe and America during past centuries? In our own interest and in the interest of world

peace we must try to convince them, by example and by practical assistance, that by using those elements of western civilization that are sound and applicable to their condition they can reach their material goals as free men while retaining the best features of their own cultures. That is why it is regrettable that Canada is budgeting to reduce its contribution to the Colombo plan at the present time.
It is important, too, that we should be honest enough and humble enough to remember that our democracy is far from complete. There is still so very much to do. Certainly it is our responsibility to make necessary adjustments in our own Canadian system of society in order more effectively to meet the needs of today. In political terms this means to be less rigid and more flexible in some of our traditonal attitudes and practices.
The most obvious fact of political life in Canada today is that Canadians are divided among five groups, four of which have substantial representation in this parliament. It is unrealistic to assume that any party represented in this house is likely to be quickly dispersed or discouraged or destroyed. An early election will only emphasize these divisions without providing a means of establishing stable government. This condition should not be viewed with alarm. Honest differences should be expected among free people. They do not constitute a danger in a mature democracy. In striving for stability, however, let us never forget that any government will become an appalling tyranny if it is not subjected to constant and unfettered scrutiny and criticism.
Our first duty, Mr. Chairman, is to recognize the problem how to manage the affairs of this nation with a minority government. This presents a challenge to all of us, government and opposition alike, to be inventive and imaginative and wise. It calls for a careful analysis of the whole concept of government and opposition. Ever since confederation we have thought mainly in terms of two major parties. The opposition has been viewed as the alternative government, ever with its eyes on the seats of power. Its constant ambition has been to "turn the rascals out", meaning, of course, the government of the day.
I submit that this part of our political heritage calls for a reappraisal at this time. In many of our political attitudes and relationships our minds are still floundering in the past. We must continually strive to lessen hostility and rivalry and to develop means of accommodation and compromise if we are to experience orderly change throughout the twentieth century and win new respect for the Canadian parliament. Jan Masaryk, the
Ways and Means
great Czechoslovakian statesman, once remarked: "Excitement is no program". That is why I submit that to view parliament as a battleground rather than as a forum for rational and responsible discussion is outmoded; it is wasteful and unintelligent and uninspiring.
Last week, when the Prime Minister intimated to us that he had consulted with the leaders of the other parties in regard to the Cuban crisis, everyone in this parliament applauded. One wonders why the same procedure could not have been followed last summer in regard to the commonwealth talks in London. Furthermore, one wonders why the same statesmanlike procedure could not be followed today in meeting the unemployment crisis, because to the man out of work unemployment is a crisis.
I suggest that we need to develop a new mood and a new technique of public administration to fit our present multiple party system. If our Canadian scientists at the defence research bureau had been content to employ nineteenth century techniques, we would never have launched a satellite and we would never have heard of "Alouette". Yet we in this house too frequently-we have evidence of this tonight-continue to think in terms of political attitudes and practices followed by Sir John A. Macdonald and George Brown 100 years ago. This is the century of technical advance. It is also the century of political innovation. Great political changes are coming in Europe and Africa and Asia. By comparison, our problem of finding a pattern for co-operative action within the Canadian parliament should not be too difficult. In any event, the present situation will test the statesmanship and ingenuity of all parties in this house in the months ahead.
Mr. Chairman, unemployment is a continuing weakness in our Canadian economy. A cure must be found if we are to be fair and just to our own people and if we are to become a strong and constructive influence in world affairs. It is an old problem. At the first trades and labour congress convention held in Canada in 1883 a resolution called for a reduction in the work week to 54 hours. Now we hear of the 35-hour week. At the turn of the century, young men found the answer to this problem by going west. But now we must face what someone has called the western wall. There are no lands beyond. We must stop and think our way through our problem. We cannot escape. The unpleasant truth is that unemployment is characteristic of Canadian society. It is a chronic condition except in wartime. Since 1945 every political party has agreed that opportunity for work is a fundamental right of Canadian citizenship

Ways and Means
and that it is a major responsibility of government to assure a high level of employment across this country. Unfortunately, words have not been matched with deeds.
We must cease being casual or complacent about it. Perhaps we are guilty of indifference, not because we are insensitive but because we are hypnotized by our affluent society. Since men and women are not starving, we are inclined to accept unemployment as something beyond our control-like the weather or the common cold. We forget, too, that when we read that there are 250,000 unemployed, we are being told that approximately one million men, women and children are living in homes where breadwinners are out of work. We hear that the number of registered unemployed has dropped a few thousand and we all feel better. I think it was the late Franklin D. Roosevelt who once remarked that it was small consolation for a man who had drowned in eight feet of water to be reminded that the average depth of the water around him was only five feet. Has Canadian statesmanship no answer to this problem? Here is a national emergency that calls for the mobilization of all our resources of leadership, not next year but today. If we wish to establish confidence in our economy we can do it only by demonstrating our ability to manage our affairs in the interest of all our people. We must combine administrative and technical efficiency with social purpose.
We are told that the government proposes to introduce a bill to provide for a national economic development board. We shall await the necessary legislation with keen interest. At present various departments are involved in dealing with different aspects of the problem of unemployment; I refer in particular to the Departments of Finance, Public Works, Labour and Trade and Commerce. It is to be hoped that the new board will be more than a consultative agency but will have broader objectives and wider powers than those exercised at present by the national productivity council. If it is to succeed it must be provided with ample staff and be given authority to take necessary steps to assure a high level of employment at all times across this country.
Industry has always planned within narrow limits. Business leaders are now talking hopefully about expanding their proven techniques into wider areas of administration.
The following comments from the Financial Post as reprinted in the Vancouver Province of August 25, 1962, are significant:
Europeans for a long time have recognized the wisdom and benefits of economic planning. Robert Fowler, president of the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association, says that Canadians also must accept

the fact that national planning to create growth and jobs is respectable and desirable.
This, as Fowler points out, will require a profoundly new approach to our economic system, to our laws and ip our attitudes. Certainly, in a business system such as ours, there is a high premium on the flexibility and foresight of individual businessmen. But because of the great changes now taking place, the most important decisions are beyond the reach of private business and in the realm of government responsibility and decision.
Last November W. S. Kirkpatrick, president of Consolidated Mining and Smelting, said this:
If one had to sum up the reason for Canada's critical economic position today, I think it could be said to be due to insufficient foresight in planning to meet the changing conditions at home and abroad.
Unless appropriate action is taken it may be questioned whether Canada's political and economic freedoms will survive the sixties.
According to the Financial Post, Mr. Kirkpatrick then suggested the formation of a new federal ministry to help set national economic goals to co-ordinate planning in this country. Labour, too, is ready for a major advance in research and co-operative action. They recognize their responsibility to share in joint consultation not only on wages and working conditions but also on problems of production, prices, and profits.
If trade unions are to perform their proper function in our democratic society they must be given opportunity to play a more positive role in the management of our Canadian economy. But government must provide leadership and direction not only in securing customers but in the more difficult and complex task of influencing investment and regulating production. Co-operation among government, labour, and management has been the key to the strengthening of the European economy since world war II. We, too, need to undertake an agonizing reappraisal of current methods in order to integrate more effectively the private and public sectors of our economy and to find a formula for stimulating industrial activity across the nation.
If the cure for unemployment threatens some of our freedoms, so does its continued presence in society. In very truth, the maintenance of full employment in a strong economy is the most effective defensive measure we could possibly contemplate in terms of human survival.
A few weeks ago we were informed by the Glassco commission that the federal government was the biggest employer in the country and, that 116 departments and agencies have a total working force of 480,000 people or approximately 7 per cent of the Canadian labour force with a total payroll of $1.8 billion. Let us now add the many thousands

employed by the ten provinces and by the countless cities and towns and local authorities from coast to coast. I am told by good authority that the figure would be in the neighbourhood of 30 per cent of the total number of men and women employed in Canada. In other words, about one in three collects his pay from a public agency. It is clear that any curtailment of this purchasing power will have a detrimental effect upon business everywhere. It follows that if the economy is to be strong, governments at all levels must behave like model employers. Only in this way can we hope to maintain a high morale and to retain competent people in the public service.
During the past summer a number of large private industries signed with their employees two year or three year agreements providing for substantial wage increases. In the interest of fair play it is to be hoped that the recommendations for improvements in the salaries of federal civil servants will soon be acted upon by this government. Certainly there should be no room in Canada for second class citizens, at least not working under this very roof.
The times demand greater attention to education for all Canadians. Practical incentives need to be provided for our young people to remain in school longer and to attend institutions of higher learning. More facilities should be available for men and women to continue their education at any age.
Employers, both in government and industry, are demanding better qualified workers. Being a pioneer people, we have assumed in the past that men could be trained on the job in a few days or weeks for any kind of employment. Failing that, an ample supply of skilled labour could be obtained in Europe just at the right time. That day has gone. In order to develop our manufacturing to the point where Canada can compete successfully throughout the world we must give serious attention to the necessity of training our own personnel.
The government is to be commended for its initiative in expanding the work of the vocational schools across the country. We welcome too the assurance of the Prime Minister that there will soon be introduced into the House of Commons legislation to provide for a major attack on the problem of automation through research and a retraining program for industrial workers. At the university level, however, Canada is not training enough students to meet the needs of industry or of the professions. The number enrolled 27507-3-68
Ways and Means
in graduate schools is dangerously low. Canadian universities award more honorary degrees to politicians than Ph.D.'s to deserving scholars. That is a sad commentary indeed on our sense of values.
In the United States and in Russia 20 per cent of the young people of college age are enrolled in some institution of higher learning. In Canada the figure is estimated to be not more than 10 per cent. In other words, only one student in 10 proceeds beyond grade 12.
Dr. Ross, president of York University, says that Canada stands a poor eleventh among the nations of the world in the number of university students according to population. That position is not good enough. We must do more to ensure that no bright young Canadian who can benefit from higher education is deprived of the opportunity through lack of money.
Our economy consumes men and machines in its productive processes. We recognize the justice of allowing tax deductions for depreciation of machinery but no similar provision is made for the replacement of men and their skills. We should at least allow income tax deductions for money spent directly by a family or an individual on education of any kind.
Our kind of democratic society calls for a maximum development of every individual as a worker and as a man. This is the task of education today. More substantial federal assistance is essential at this critical period in history without in any way lessening the authority of the provinces in the broad field of educational administration.
Already the federal government is involved in a broad program of education and culture that reaches into a dozen different departments. Some form of liaison is needed both for efficiency and for convenience. The sensible solution seems to be a central office of education to be administered jointly by federal and provincial governments. Such a development could stimulate a young and vigorous Canada to take its rightful place in the battle for men's minds that is being waged across the world at the present time.
In recent years, through channels provided by the C.B.C. and the Canada Council, young people in the field of the arts have received opportunities for training and travel previously denied them. As a result, an increasing number of Canadian artists are serving as goodwill ambassadors abroad. In a modest way, it is true to say that Canada has become an exporter of culture as well as of wheat and newsprint.

Ways and Means
For these reasons, I suggest that the government should consider establishing, in co-operation with the provinces, a federal office of education to perform the following services:
1.	To direct more efficiently the educational activities of approximately 75,000 students at present attending federally operated schools, at a cost of $50 million annually.
2.	To administer a program of research and retraining of workers required to meet the demands of automation.
3.	To encourage and publicize the comprehensive programs of adult education at present offered by Canadian universities.
4.	To act as a clearing house for the matching grants now paid to the provinces for such services as student loans and scholarships, special courses for new Canadians, handicapped children, apprentices, unemployed, etc.
5.	To provide a medium for the distribution among provinces of information resulting from research studies and experiments conducted at the local level by school or university authorities.
6.	To promote greater understanding among educators through the exchange of teachers from one province to another.
7.	To co-ordinate the educational work of the Canada council, national research council, Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and UNESCO.
Few will deny that maximum use of our resources can produce a finer generation of citizens than we have ever known-healthier, better educated, more appreciative of the arts, and more aware of one another. Recently the Canadian novelist, Professor Hugh McLennan of McGill University, wrote as follows:
The Canadian of today has climbed and been pushed to the highest material plateau any Canadian of any year has ever reached. But above him tower the really interesting ranges, and only if he reaches them will it matter to mankind whether or not he ever existed.
Who cares today how much corn the Athenians ate in the sixth decade of the fourth century B.C. or how much money they made out of their mercantile marine?
But for more than 2,000 years men have greatly cared that it was in the sixth decade of that century that the building of the Parthenon was begun and that Sophocles wrote Antigone.
Without the corn crop, without the silver, without the Mediterranean trade, Athens would not have been able to build the Parthenon or maintain at public expense the theatres for those plays that made her immortal.
But the reason she is immortal, the reason she is priceless to mankind, is that the Athenian citizen did not consider the production, distribution and consumption of material goods an end in itself, but only a necessary means to the far greater end of making his city one in which mature and civilized personalities could live joyful and exciting lives.

I submit that in this country we need a greater ambition than to create a favourable economic and political environment in order to attract investment and industry, in other words, to become bigger and bigger and richer and richer. Will Canadians in the future be content to brag about their highways and bridges, their factories and skyscrapers? Or will they be inspired to reach out for other goals, for new values and new standards of excellence in human achievement? Let us not forget that it is still true that we grow like what we worship.
Among thoughtful people throughout the western world today, there is a strong conviction that material prosperity by itself is an insecure foundation on which to build a civilization. I am convinced that to survive western democracy must grow not only in administrative efficiency and technical skill but also in social justice and moral strength.
We need at times to climb to higher ground, as Hugh McLennan has advised, and consider how we can so manage the affairs of this nation that ever increasing numbers of people will come to know the meaning of creative and joyous living.

Mr. Chairman, since this is the first opportunity I have had to do so, let me join in the many other congratulations that you have received on your appointment. Your fairness and desire to live up to the high requirements demanded by your office have already impressed not only newer members such as myself but also every other member of the house.
The speech by the Associate Minister of National Defence has helped to prove more than anything else we have yet seen in the house the deceit, the half truths and the outright fraud of which this present government is guilty.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Do not forget this is your maiden speech.
Leave him alone.

I will say to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi that he is a wonderful example of something different from the usual trend of people becoming smarter as they get older. He seems to be depreciating in his intelligence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This is your maiden speech.

We have had an example tonight, Mr. Chairman, of the colossal nerve which the government displays; but they will not get away with it on this occasion. The Associate Minister of National Defence took the latest issue of Time magazine and quoted certain passages from an article about the Canadian economy, but he left out certain

more important quotations. For example, on the very same page from which the Associate Minister of National Defence quoted we read these words:
"We're prosperous, but slowly going bankrupt," a Toronto economist wryly reflected. "This is a special Canadian trick."
I quote again from this article:
What Diefenbaker did not go out of his way to mention was that some key indicators are unhappily slowing up. The index of industrial production rose steeply to 186.6 in May, from 169.2 a year earlier, but slowed to a crawl by midsummer. Unemployment, while lower than it has been, was still, at 3.9 per cent of the labour force, not low enough. A 4 per cent rise in public spending during the first six months, mostly on a crash program to build vocational schools, was flattened by Ottawa's $228 million austerity cut-back-"and that," said a Montreal economist, "is $228 million worth of jobs."
That is what they did not say, Mr. Chairman, and I hope that in the next campaign, which I think will be soon, the Associate Minister of National Defence will come into the Essex ridings and make this very same type of speech before the unemployed automobile workers of Windsor. He will do myself and my other Liberal colleagues of the county of Essex a great favour and he will give us a lot of help in getting re-elected.
This has been bad enough, Mr. Chairman, these half truths, this failure to quote these passages from the very page from which the minister quoted in his speech, but we have seen something worse; and this is all the worse because so far hon. gentlemen opposite have not even seemed to notice this particular omission. I would have thought, Mr. Chairman, that the very first thing the associate minister of defence would have done in beginning his speech would have been to dissociate himself completely from the vile words quoted by the hon. member for Laurier.
Oh, oh.

You may be laughing at this, but that is just proof of what I am saying. Because of his failure to dissociate himself from these words, he has given proof to the millions of immigrants in this country, to the people of the same religious background as those referred to in this vile article, that everything these hon. gentlemen opposite have said about their bill of rights is a despicable sham and an attempt to get votes.
That is a filthy lie.
Let me tell you something, and I refer to the hon. member opposite-

Hamilton South.
27507-3-68J
Ways and Means
-the hon. member for Hamilton South, that I happen to share the racial background and religious beliefs of the people to whom reference is made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Get on with your speech.

That is all you can say. I hope this will be repeated and recorded so that the people whose parents have come from the other side of the ocean, as mine did, will know, even better than they did before, exactly where hon. members opposite actually stand when it comes to the question of civil rights. We are being shown this more clearly than we were ever shown it before.
Keep religion out of politics.

You should refer to the minister who has just spoken because he brought it in in the worst possible way by failing to dissociate himself from those vile words quoted by the hon. member for Laurier.
While Cuba may be a crisis point in world affairs, Mr. Chairman, there are also crises points here in Canadian affairs, crises points which the present Conservative government has shown a reluctance and an inability to deal with in any meaningful way.
One of the new Liberal statesmen.
If I am a new Liberal statesman I hope God will give me the strength to do a better job than hon. gentlemen opposite have done.
You will certainly need His help.

One of the problems with which we are faced is chronic unemployment, and all the boasting of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister about more people working and more jobs cannot obscure the fact that there is a condition of continuing unemployment declining in many areas across Canada. In the Windsor area, for example, there has been a decline since 1957 of some 9,000 industrial jobs, jobs not replaced in any way by any serious measures of the present government which, all along, has pretended, and unfortunately continues to pretend, that this problem of chronic unemployment in certain of the areas of our nation does not really exist.
The people of the Windsor area listened to the speeches of the Prime Minister, and those of hon. gentlemen opposite, during the past campaign in which he claimed to put everything, including his party's record of achievement, fully and frankly before them. Having listened, sir, they made up their minds and passed judgment on the Prime Minister and

Ways and Means
his party by decisively rejecting his candidates at the polls. I would suggest that they did so, at least in part, because they saw that this government had no real program for dealing with continuing unemployment. They lacked, and still lack, a program to deal with the threat to jobs created by changing technology, automation and by the movement of industry.
We Liberals have a program in this regard and we have continued to develop it. The hon. member for Davenport and others have put some of its details and approaches before you. Mind you, from this program the government has attempted to take a few bright threads to dress up the shabby cloth of its throne speech. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and others have appeared to suggest that the throne speech held out hopes of a rich and nourishing banquet of legislation. Instead, we have had only the stale porridge of last April's budget resolutions barely warmed over by the personal charm of the Minister of Finance.
The throne speech referred to an Atlantic development board. Surely, by now it must be obvious even to hon. gentlemen seated opposite that what we need and must have is not just a board to deal with one region, with other problem areas remaining almost completely ignored. Instead, we must have a new agency for area redevelopment, concerning itself with and administering a vital program not only to bring progress to the Windsor area but to all these other areas in the country. These projects must be applicable to the country as a whole; they must be meaningful and comprehensive, not just bits and pieces that have no meaningful purpose other than to dress up the Conservative campaign literature.
I believe the Prime Minister spoke of public works being carried out to aid certain areas in alleviating unemployment. Can he or the Minister of Public Works tell the committee when his government will permit at last a harbour development in the Windsor area? Can there be any real explanation given other than the present government's incompetence, its lack of concern for the constituency of Essex West.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I want to ask the hon. member what he is reading from. He has been reading from this piece of paper for the last ten minutes.
Shame on you; it is his maiden speech.

With reference to the hon. gentleman's interjection, I may say I am referring very briefly from time to time to

certain notes. Perhaps if he had the opportunity of reading these notes he would make a much more serious and constructive statement in this house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He must be nearsighted.

Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, I have to wear glasses. However, I am not so nearsighted that I cannot see the emptiness of the Conservative program.
To continue, Mr. Chairman, I ask why the present government has provided nothing for harbour development in Windsor, on the busiest waterway in the world, when it has been spending hundreds of thousands of dollars, and continues to spend that money, in spite of its austerity program, for such works in cities and towns with less population than Windsor and less shipping business than Windsor has right now. The great American city of Detroit, with its population of almost three million, is on the other side of the riverbed. Now, its lack of port facilities has, at times in the past, made it necessary for ships to line up three or four in a row in the Detroit river waiting for space to dock on the United States side. A harbour in the Windsor area with appropriate bonded warehouse facilities might create not only a much needed source of employment but also provide a way to earn United States dollars. Something must be done now before this opportunity has disappeared.
The failure to carry out measures of this type, Mr. Chairman, shows the basic mistakes of the present government in dealing with the financial crisis they have done so much to create. They have failed to create what I might call productive of public works which would help to create permanent jobs and industry once those works were completed. The present Conservative government has failed completely to deal with the problem of movement of industry, the movement of plants from certain communities especially dependant upon them and without other plants to take their place. This problem should be one of grave concern not only to the communities involved but also to all of Canada, since their decline threatens the progress of the entire country.
This problem, Mr. Chairman, has its economic aspects when industries concentrate so heavily in the few great metropolitan areas of Canada. This concentration puts a tremendous burden on them to provide expensive services both for these plants and for the expanding population. At the same time, once these industries have moved, these towns and cities are left with the problems and burdens of paying, with declining tax

revenues, for these services once required for these industries and the homes of their workers. Specific mention must be made, Mr. Chairman, of the continuing burden on these municipalities, together with the provincial and federal government and therefore on all Canadians, of maintaining those who are turned into the chronic unemployed from changes in technology, changes in the economy and especially these plant movements. This is a human problem, Mr. Chairman, as well as an economic one. There is a humanitarian aspect to all this, probably more significant in final analysis than the economic one.
It seems to me that there is a basic inhumanity in taking a man who may have devoted a lifetime to a company and throwing him on the scrap heap like an outmoded machine-a man who may well be too old by today's narrow standards and lacking the necessary technical skills to find another job in his own city, if one were available, or anywhere else for that matter. This man may have put his life savings into a home. He may have built up the network of friendships and associations which one naturally creates over a lifetime in a community. What is a man like this to do? He will probably have difficulty at his age and level of skill in finding another job. If he has a chance to move with the same company to its new location-and this does not happen often enough -who will buy his home at a fair price? If he wishes to go elsewhere and find work, who will help ease the burden of moving expenses and of maintaining himself and his family while he is finding that job? Who will help him learn another skill so that he may fit into our changing technology before his present job disappears?
I regret to say that I have reached the conclusion that the companies concerned have as yet not assumed their proper share of their responsibilities to the worker who has given years of his life in their service, or to the cities which have become dependant on those plants and have gone into debt to serve them. There is a great task to be performed here. Of course, to deal completely with this problem we must have the co-operation of the provincial and federal governments. But the federal government has wide powers of its own which it must put into use immediately to deal with these crucial problems of depressed areas and industrial location. There is much more that could or should be done to help workers to bear the expense of finding new jobs in another area. There is much that can and should be done not only to train those who are now unemployed, but to train others who are now working for these
Ways and Means
new jobs created by changing technology, before that technology destroys the jobs they now have. But most important of all there must be a comprehensive and dynamic program along the lines set forth by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Davenport to bring new industry and new jobs to the Atlantic provinces, to Windsor and to all areas in need of special development aid, as well as a program to help maintain existing industry in those areas. In short, we need a program using the full existing powers of the federal government to create an economic climate in which both new and existing industries can prosper and expand, creating new jobs in the areas where they are really necessary.
A one-way rail ticket was your answer.

I am not sure which corner of the wrong side of the house that comment came from, but I feel I should refer at this point to the views of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands who, I believe, on October 23 last criticized most severely the sound proposals of the hon. member for Davenport to increase industrial activity through incentives, submitting those proposals to a bitter and scathing attack. First of all, I must compliment the hon. member and give him credit for his personal honesty and integrity-his courage in forthrightly announcing that he is a socialist, and an unreconstructed one at that. While I do not share his views on that score, I must acknowledge how different his attitude from that of some other members of his party who go to great lengths to remove what they must consider to be the taint of socialism from their policies, their statements and even the name of their party.
I want to refer hon. members briefly to some of the comments he made in the course of his bitter and scathing attack on the hon. member for Davenport. I am referring to Hansard for Tuesday, October 23. After saying he was an unreconstructed socialist, the hon. member went on to say he was-
-more convinced today than I was 30 years ago that the solutions to the problems of our nation cannot be found within the framework of private enterprise, of capitalism, of the business world.
As reported on page 852, after referring to the brutal despotisms of what is termed the communist world, he goes on to refer to the need for revolutionary change to sweep away-
-the more subtle despotisms of the democratic world, the world of private enterprise.
Again, as recorded on page 852, he says:
As we build the new institutions we must begin the demolition of the old.

Ways and Means
Mr. Chairman, I wondered when I heard this, which institutions he had in mind destroying. I certainly hope he was not thinking of the democratic institutions of which this wonderful house is the embodiment.
Then, as reported on the same page, the hon. member said:
We can have no part in attempts to plaster over the widening cracks in the capitalist structure.
This attack on every section of private enterprise must have sent shudders down the spines of those in the hon. member's party who have been trying in a conciliatory fashion to woo small business and imply there is space within its confines even for the small businessman. I am sure the old timers in this house must for a moment have thought they were back in the days of the Regina manifesto and not the scrubbed up program the N.D.P. is trying to peddle today.
Since this particular hon. member has been described by the Canadian Press as his party's financial critic, I decided to take another look at his party's so-called program to see what it could add to his ideas. Either the hon. member in his speech has signalled a major policy change on behalf of his party or he was off on an ideological frolic of his own from which, perhaps, Mr. Douglas will recall him when he takes his seat in this house. For example, I would refer to a pamphlet entitled "A Summary of the New Democratic Program". Under the heading "Industry", it says:
A program to locate industry-if necessary, a whole new industrial complex-in communities which today face the prospect of continued economic distress. Through genuine incentives to industries seeking new sites, by lending money at low interest rates for the initiation of industrial and manufacturing projects-
Then again, looking at the actual program, at page 10 under the heading "Area Redevelopment", I see the following:
Special attention will be given to a location of industry policy, similar to successful programs in Britain, Sweden and other countries. This policy will include tax concessions and other assistance to private industry, as well as public investment.
I may say that I gave a lot of publicity to this program during the election, and I think that is a good reason why I am in this house today. No wonder the people of Canada have been unable to take seriously either the program or the party of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, who, apparently, is its financial spokesman.
But to get back to the question of chronic unemployment. There is an urgent task which faces our federal government-a task bound up with encouraging subsidiaries of United States-owned firms to produce more of their products in Canada. The hon. member for

Davenport has made reference to our automobile industry and voiced an opinion, which I share, that we could produce more of our own cars than we do today. Apparently, the constant urging and prodding of we Liberals has now forced the Minister of Finance to begin to share this view. We listened with great interest to the hon. gentleman's statement today. I want to point out again that it has taken two long years for the government finally to decide to do something about beginning to implement the main recommendations of Dr. Bladen's report. The measures announced today are, at best, a start. They are only a superficial attempt to deal with the broad problem of finding means to make more of our cars in Canada.
It is perhaps somewhat early to comment in detail on the implications of this statement and on the likely results of the order in council. We shall have to see what approach is taken by the automobile companies and by the United States parent firms. Let us hope they will make use of the provisions to increase the manufacture of automobile parts in Canada. I certainly hope they will not decide to continue importing transmissions, paying the duty and passing on the cost to the Canadian consumer, though there may be some risk of this happening. We must continue to look at all possible ways of increasing the Canadian content in our automobiles. One challenging and thought provoking suggestion of how this might be done was made several weeks ago by Mr. .Gray-biel, the general manager of the Windsor Star, when he suggested, in effect, that we have a crown corporation if our own automobile companies do not want to do this.
This suggestion is certainly deserving of further study, and has already brought forth comments by certain segments of our automobile industry as to the impracticability and impossibility of manufacturing these transmissions here.
It is easy to see why the United States parent firms should resist attempts to have transmissions made here. After all, they probably derive some substantial economic benefit through selling transmissions to their Canadian subsidiaries, without the cost of setting up such plants in Canada. Let us remember that there are many countries which have much more stringent requirements as to local content than does Canada. I merely want to point out, without necessarily voicing any approval of any of these requirements, that many of these great United States companies not only have subsidiaries operating in these countries, but in many cases they have made substantial increases in their investments in the recent past and probably plan further investment in the future.

Many of these countries offer very little in comparison with Canada when it comes to the existing markets, but quite a number of these United States companies have a potential market, and in spite of these requirements these United States companies have not only set up plants but are increasing their investment. Canada, on the other hand, is one of the major automobile markets outside of the United States itself.
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if we can take measures whereby we would insist upon the greater manufacture of automobile parts in Canada, it would be in the Canadian national interest and would create jobs for Canadians. Then with our encouragement our automobile companies will, I feel certain, be able to find, as they have done elsewhere, satisfactory means to comply not only with government measures, but will also be able to operate to their own benefit and, more important, to the increased benefit of Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, one of the most important reasons for helping the depressed areas of Canada is that in so doing we will permit them to make a real contribution once again to Canadian life. In the riding of Essex West we find representatives of every group that make up the Canadian mosaic.
(Translation):
Thus, I am very proud that in my riding of Essex West, the old tradition of French language and culture is still going strong. That is why I am proud to further that tradition in the house where the two major language groups of our country are represented.
In Windsor, in the riding of Essex West, English speaking and French speaking Canadians show a spirit of understanding and good will which sets an example for the rest of Canada.
(Text):
Mr. Chairman, Essex West and Windsor can serve as examples to Canada in many ways; in the friendliness of its people, in the way these people of many religious and origins live together in a spirit of tolerance and understanding. In many other ways up until now Windsor has been the setter of patterns, the pacemaker for the rest of Canada.
Hear, hear.

Here is a man who knows. It has been a pacemaker of secondary industry, a place where labour has contributed to the development of workers throughout Canada. But may I also predict that Windsor will set a new national pattern for new high levels of productivity and labour-management cooperation so that Windsor, with the assistance of the federal government will be able to
Ways and Means
show the rest of the country the way to remove this crisis of chronic unemployment from our national life so that we may take the steps that must be taken to put Canada back on the path of national greatness in a world of prosperity and freedom.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member for Essex West permit one question?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry, but the time of the hon. member for Essex West has expired.

Mr. Chairman, we have heard this evening the maiden speech of the hon. member for Essex West. He seems to be following in the footsteps of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres. He talks about fraud by political parties in this country. He apparently did not read the newspapers in 1956 when a supposed great gentleman trampled parliament to death, not only selling it to big industry, but to United States big industry, giving them extra options for the pipe line across the country.
The hon. member talked about the Associate Minister of National Defence not ridiculing hon. members in the corner, this man who walks around in sheer proof of his contempt of the system that he fought against during the war. The hon. member talks about the Liberal party which wants to weld Canada together. He talks about the Mackenzie King theory of divide and conquer. He should think about conscription for a moment.
I did not say anything about that.

The hon.
members says he never talked about this. He implied it, which is the usual Liberal party way of doing things. They are so flexible that they walk the tightrope and fall off whichever way is convenient. Now it is socialism. They talk about crown corporations and automobile parts. They talk about Windsor, and say nothing has happened there. We had a member of the cabinet in the Liberal government in 1935 up to 1957. What happened then?
The Liberal government set up the harbour commission. You did not give them any money.

The proof is in the pudding. I have listened to the hon. member from Essex West. He gets up and talks of the automobile industry in Windsor, the border city. I feel that if there is some criticism to make about the development of Windsor harbour, he had better talk to the

Ways and Means
gentleman who is sitting next to him at the present time. Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock.
You are going to force me to make a speech.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. gentleman a question? In view of the remarks of the hon. member for Essex West, does the hon. member know that the Ottawa Journal, in an editorial today commenting upon this debate, said that the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands made one of the few worth-while contributions to this debate?
He did not hear the hon. member for Essex West.

Ten o'clock.
Progress reported.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I inquire what we will be doing tomorrow, and perhaps we could get some indication of the business for the rest of the week.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a continuation of the committee of ways and means is all I can foresee at the moment. It depends upon the members of the opposition.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If we should conclude, will we go on with the items mentioned on Friday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is a hypothetical question. I do not know whether we will conclude tomorrow.
The government is confused.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, Oclober 30, 1962
